chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter is a journey through five ideas: counting in groups, landmark numbers, a base, place value and zero. Each number system is used, not just looked at: students write numbers in it, add in it and find where it breaks, so that the next idea arrives as the fix for a real difficulty.

points.title: Use each system before judging it
points.text: Every system is met through writing and adding numbers in it, and its weakness is found by trying a number it cannot handle.

points.title: Tools only where handling is the idea
points.text: Nine tools, each used once: matching sticks to tally marks, building names and Roman numerals, reading Egyptian symbols, grouping counters into a base, regrouping on a counting board, a base 60 place board, holding an empty place, and sorting number systems by their features.

points.title: Our own symbols for strange numerals
points.text: Picture numerals are always read back into Hindu numerals with the grouping written out, so the structure is clear even when the symbols are new.

points.title: History as a story, not a list
points.text: Reema and her father carry the story; dates and names are context, and the chapter keeps asking what problem each new idea solved.

concepts.concept_name: A loose page of strange symbols

content.text:
3.1 Reema's Curiosity
One lazy afternoon, Reema was flipping through an old book when, whoosh!, a piece of paper slipped out and floated to the floor. She picked it up and stared at the strange symbols all over it. "What is this?" she wondered.
She ran to her father, holding the paper as if it were a secret treasure. He looked at it and smiled. "Around 4000 years ago, there flourished a civilisation in a region called Mesopotamia, in the western part of Asia, containing a major part of the present-day Iraq and a few other neighbouring countries. This is one of the ways they wrote their numbers!"
Reema's eyes lit up, "Seriously? These strange symbols were numbers?"
Since when have humans been counting? What was their need for counting? What were they counting?
Since when have people been writing numbers in the modern form?
How would the Mesopotamians have written 20? 50? 100?

4. Keep the last question open: how would those people have written 20, 50 or 100? We answer it in the last part of the chapter.

content.text:
Humans had the need to count even as early as the Stone Age. They were counting to determine the quantity of food they had, the number of animals in their livestock, details regarding trades of goods, the number of offerings given in rituals, etc.
Ancient Indian texts, such as the Yajurveda Samhita, mentioned names of numbers based on powers of 10, almost as we say them orally today. For example, they listed names for the numbers one (eka), ten (dasha), hundred (shata), thousand (sahasra), ten thousand (ayuta), etc., all the way up to 10 to the power 12 and beyond.
The first known instance of numbers being written using ten digits, including the digit 0 (which was then notated as a dot), occurs in the Bakhshali manuscript (c. 3rd century CE).
The Indian number system was transmitted to the Arab world by around 800 CE.
From the Arab world, the Hindu numerals were transmitted to Europe and to parts of Africa by around 1100 CE.
"The ingenious method of expressing every possible number using a set of ten symbols (each symbol having a place value and an absolute value) emerged in India." (Pierre-Simon Laplace)
The most commonly used terminologies for the numbers we use today are 'Hindu numerals', 'Indian numerals', and the transitional 'Hindu-Arabic numerals'.
The shape of the digits 0, 1, 2, ..., 9 used to write numbers in the Indian number system today evolved over a period of time.

content.text:
Worked example: The Yajurveda lists eka, dasha, shata, sahasra and ayuta. Which numbers are these, and how is each one related to the one before it?
1. eka is one and dasha is ten: 10 × 1 = 10.
2. shata is a hundred: 10 × 10 = 100.
3. sahasra is a thousand: 10 × 100 = 1000.
4. ayuta is ten thousand: 10 × 1000 = 10000.
5. Each name is 10 times the one before it, so the names follow powers of 10, just as we say numbers today.
Answer: 1, 10, 100, 1000 and 10000; each is 10 times the one before

concepts.concept_name: One stick for every cow: one-to-one mapping

content.text:
The Mechanism of Counting
Imagine that we are living in the Stone Age, say, around ten thousand years ago. Suppose we have a herd of cows.
Q1. How do we ensure that all cows have returned safely after grazing? Q2. Do we have fewer cows than our neighbour? Q3. If there are fewer, how many more cows would we need so that we have the same number of cows as our neighbour?
Method 1: We could tackle the questions by using pebbles, sticks or any object that is available in abundance. Let us choose sticks. For every cow in the herd, we could keep a stick.
This way of associating each cow with a stick, such that no two cows are associated or mapped to the same stick is called a one-to-one mapping.
How will you use such sticks to answer the other two questions (Q2 and Q3)?

content.text:
1. Predict first: with no number names at all, can you tell whether every cow came home?
2. Keep one stick for each cow in the morning. In the evening, take one stick out for each cow that returns.
3. A stick left over means a cow is missing; this pairing, one cow to one stick, is a one-to-one mapping.
4. To compare with a neighbour, pair your sticks with theirs: the unpaired sticks show who has more and how many more are needed.

content.text:
Worked example: In the morning a herder keeps one stick for each cow. In the evening she takes out one stick for each cow that returns, and 2 sticks are left. Her neighbour's stick bundle, paired stick by stick with hers, has 3 sticks without partners. What can she say?
1. Each returning cow removes exactly one stick, so every stick left stands for a cow that did not return.
2. 2 sticks are left, so 2 cows are still missing.
3. Pairing her sticks with the neighbour's sticks one to one, the 3 unpaired sticks are on the neighbour's side.
4. So she has fewer cows than her neighbour, and she needs 3 more cows to have the same number.
Answer: 2 cows are missing; she has fewer cows than her neighbour and needs 3 more

concepts.concept_name: Letters and symbols as a counting sequence

content.text:
Method 2: Instead of objects, we could use a standard sequence of sounds or names. For example, we could use the sounds of the letters of any language.
An obvious limitation of using only the letters of the English alphabet in this form is that it cannot be used to count collections having more than 26 objects.
How many numbers can you represent in this way using the sounds of the letters of your language?
Method 3: We could use a sequence of written symbols as follows.
I, II, III, IV, V, VI, VII, VIII, IX, X, XI, XII, XIII, XIV, XV, XVI, XVII, XVIII, XIX, XX (Table 1)
Do you see a way of extending this method to represent bigger numbers as well? How?

1. Predict first: using the letters a to z, which letter goes with the 20th object?

concepts.concept_name: A number system is a standard sequence

content.text:
For counting and finding the size of a collection, we need a standard sequence of objects, or names, or written symbols, that has a fixed order. Let us call this standard sequence a number system.
Since there is no end to numbers, the challenge is to come up with an unending standard sequence/number system that is easy to count with.
Using sticks gives an unending standard sequence/number system. However, it is not convenient to count larger collections, as we will need as many sticks as the number of objects being counted.
The standard sequence/number system given in Method 3 was actually the system used in Europe before it got replaced by the Hindu number system. It is called the Roman number system.
The symbols occurring in a written number system are called numerals.

content.text:
Worked example: Compare the three counting methods (sticks, letters a to z, Roman symbols) on two questions: does the sequence ever end, and is it easy to count a large collection with it?
1. Sticks: add one more stick each time, so the sequence never ends; but 500 cows need 500 sticks, which is slow and heavy.
2. Letters: easy to say quickly, but after z there is no next letter, so it ends at 26.
3. Roman symbols: compact, but bigger and bigger numbers keep needing new symbols.
4. None of the three is both unending and easy; that is the challenge a good number system must meet.
Answer: Sticks never end but are slow; letters are quick but end at 26; Roman symbols need ever new symbols

content.text:
Figure it Out (the mechanism of counting, question 1): Suppose you are using the number system that uses sticks to represent numbers, as in Method 1. Without using either the number names or the numerals of the Hindu number system, give a method for adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing two numbers or two collections of sticks.
1. To add, put the two collections of sticks together; the joined pile is the sum.
2. To subtract, pair each stick of the smaller pile with a stick of the larger pile and take the pairs away; the unpaired sticks are the difference.
3. To multiply, lay out the first pile once for every stick of the second pile and join all the copies.
4. To divide, keep taking out groups the size of the second pile; the number of groups is the quotient and the sticks that cannot make a full group are the remainder.
Answer: Add by joining, subtract by pairing and removing, multiply by repeating one pile once per stick of the other, divide by taking out equal groups

subtracting: pair sticks of the smaller pile with sticks of the larger pile, stick by stick, and take the pairs away; the unpaired sticks are what is left
multiplying: lay out the first pile once for every stick of the second pile and join all the copies
dividing: keep taking out a group the size of the second pile from the first; the number of groups is the answer and sticks that cannot fill a group are the leftover

content.text:
Figure it Out (the mechanism of counting, question 2): One way of extending the number system in Method 2 is by using strings with more than one letter, for example, we could use 'aa' for 27. How can you extend this system to represent all the numbers? There are many ways of doing it!
1. After z, start again with doubled letters: aa, bb, cc, ..., zz count the next 26 objects.
2. Then use tripled letters aaa, bbb, ..., zzz for the next 26, and so on.
3. Another way: after z use aa, ab, ac, ..., az, then ba, bb, ..., like the columns of a spreadsheet.
4. Either way, longer strings can always be made, so the sequence never runs out.
Answer: One way: a to z, then aa, bb, ..., zz, then aaa, bbb, ..., zzz and so on; many other ways work

content.text:
Figure it Out (the mechanism of counting, question 3): Try making your own number system.
1. Choose a standard sequence with a fixed order: objects, sounds or written marks.
2. Check that it never runs out: decide how to make the next symbol after any symbol.
3. Check that it is easy to count with: for example, give a new mark to every group of five.
4. Test it by writing a few numbers, such as the number of students in your class.
Answer: Open answer: any fixed-order sequence that never runs out and is easy to count with

content.text:
3.2 Some Early Number Systems
I. Use of Body Parts: Many groups of people across the world have used their hands and body parts for counting.
II. Tally Marks on Bones and Other Surfaces: One of the oldest methods of number representation is by making notches, marks cut on a surface such as a bone or a wall of a cave. These marks are also called tally marks.
In this method, a mark is made for each object that is being counted.
The Lebombo bone, discovered in South Africa, is an even older tally stick with 29 notches, estimated to be around 44,000 years old.

2. Body-part counting points to fingers, wrist, elbow, shoulder and so on, in a fixed order.
3. A tally makes one mark for each object, just like keeping one stick for each cow.
4. Long rows of marks are hard to read, which is why people began to bunch them in groups.

content.text:
Worked example: The Lebombo bone has 29 notches. Group them in fives. How many full groups are there, and how many notches are left over?
1. Count off five notches at a time: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25.
2. That is 5 full groups of five, and 5 × 5 = 25.
3. 29 − 25 = 4, so 4 notches are left over.
4. So the 29 notches read as 5 groups of five and 4 more: 5 × 5 + 4 = 29.
Answer: 5 groups of five and 4 more

III. Number Names Obtained by Counting in Twos
A group of indigenous people in Australia called the Gumulgal had the following words for their numbers: 1 urapon, 2 ukasar, 3 ukasar-urapon, 4 ukasar-ukasar, 5 ukasar-ukasar-urapon, 6 ukasar-ukasar-ukasar.
The numbers are counted in 2s, using which the number names are formed: 3 = 2 + 1, 4 = 2 + 2, 5 = 2 + 2 + 1, 6 = 2 + 2 + 2.
Gumulgal called any number greater than 6 ras.
Despite being so far apart geographically, and with no trace of contact between them, these three groups have developed equivalent number systems!

content.text:
Worked example: In the Gumulgal system, urapon is 1 and ukasar is 2. Build the names for 5 and 6, and say what a Gumulgal speaker would say for 7.
1. Split 5 into twos and a one: 5 = 2 + 2 + 1.
2. So 5 is ukasar-ukasar-urapon.
3. 6 = 2 + 2 + 2, so 6 is ukasar-ukasar-ukasar.
4. Any number greater than 6 was simply called ras.
Answer: 5 is ukasar-ukasar-urapon, 6 is ukasar-ukasar-ukasar, and 7 is ras

concepts.concept_name: Grouping by one size, and its limit

content.text:
A general form which this idea has taken in different number systems is as follows: count in groups of a certain number (like 2 in the case of Gumulgal's system), and use the word or symbol associated with this group size to represent bigger numbers.
Some of the commonly used group sizes in different number systems have been 2, 5, 10 and 20.
Up to what group size could you immediately see the number of objects without counting? Most humans find it difficult to count groups having 5 or more objects in a single glance.
What could be the difficulties with using a number system that counts only in groups of a single particular size? How would you represent a number like 1345 in a system that counts only by 5s?

content.text:
1. Predict first: how many dots can you see at a glance without counting, 3, 6 or 10?
2. Most people see up to about 4 at once; 5 or more need counting, so marks were bunched in fives.
3. Counting in groups of one size, such as 2 or 5, shortens a long row of marks.
4. But a large number still needs a huge number of groups, so one group size alone is not enough.

content.text:
Worked example: In a system that counts only by 5s, how would 1345 be written? How many group symbols are needed?
1. Find how many fives make 1345: 1345 ÷ 5 = 269.
2. Check: 269 × 5 = 1345, so nothing is left over.
3. So 1345 needs the symbol for five written 269 times.
4. That is far too many symbols to write or read, so a single group size soon becomes cumbersome.
Answer: 269 symbols for five, too many to write or read easily

content.text:
Figure it Out (early number systems, question 1): A group of indigenous people in a Pacific island use different sequences of number names to count different objects. Why do you think they do this?
1. Think about what was being counted: fish, coconuts, canoes, days.
2. Things that come in bunches or pairs may be easier to count in their own groups.
3. A separate sequence also tells the listener what kind of object is meant.
4. So the sequences may follow how each kind of object is usually grouped, traded or used.
Answer: Open answer: for example, each kind of object is grouped or traded in its own way, and the name also tells what is being counted

media.description: A system that counts only in groups of five needs one symbol for every group. The video divides 1345 by 5 to find how many symbols are needed, and checks the count by putting the groups back. Keeko's doubt is that fives make the row short.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students describe counting with body parts and with tally marks on bones, and group the 29 notches of the Lebombo bone into fives to read them faster.
Students explain how the Gumulgal names for 3 to 6 are built from urapon (1) and ukasar (2), and build the name for a number up to 6.
Students find the group size they can see at a glance, explain why tally marks were bunched in fives, and show that counting 1345 in fives alone still needs 269 groups.
Students explain why some people use different counting sequences for different objects, and add, subtract, multiply and divide numbers written in the Gumulgal system extended beyond 6.

content.text:
Figure it Out (early number systems, question 2): Consider the extension of the Gumulgal number system beyond 6 in the same way of counting by 2s. Come up with ways of performing the different arithmetic operations (+, −, ×, ÷) for numbers occurring in this system, without using Hindu numerals. Use this to evaluate the following: (i) (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-urapon) + (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-urapon) (ii) (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-urapon) − (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar) (iii) (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-urapon) × (ukasar-ukasar) (iv) (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar) ÷ (ukasar-ukasar)
1. (i) Join the words: 4 ukasar and 3 ukasar give 7 ukasar, and the two urapons make one more ukasar, so 8 ukasar. Check: 9 + 7 = 16.
2. (ii) Take 3 ukasar away from 4 ukasar and an urapon: ukasar-urapon is left. Check: 9 − 6 = 3.
3. (iii) ukasar-ukasar is two twos, so write the first number two times and then double the result, 4 copies in all: 16 ukasar and 4 urapons, and the 4 urapons make 2 more ukasar, so 18 ukasar. Check: 9 × 4 = 36.
4. (iv) Share 8 ukasar into groups of ukasar-ukasar: there are 4 groups, written ukasar-ukasar. Check: 16 ÷ 4 = 4.
Answer: (i) ukasar written 8 times (ii) ukasar-urapon (iii) ukasar written 18 times (iv) ukasar-ukasar

media.description: The Gumulgal number names are carried past six by counting in twos. The video adds, subtracts, multiplies and divides four given numbers using only the words ukasar and urapon, and checks each answer with ordinary number words.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: a number counted in twos is a row of ukasar with an urapon at the end if one is left over, and two urapon make one more ukasar. Each operation works on the row of words. Watch for students who convert to Hindu numerals before they begin.

concepts.concept_name: Group a number into landmark numbers

content.text:
IV. The Roman Numerals
To get the Roman numeral for any number till 39, it is first grouped into as many 10s as possible, the remaining is grouped into as many 5s as possible, and finally the remaining is grouped into 1s.
Example: Let us take the number 27. 27 = 10 + 10 + 5 + 1 + 1. So, 27 in Roman numerals is XXVII.
Instead of representing 50 as XXXXX, a new symbol is given to it: L. Following the way the number 4 is represented as 1 less than 5, that is, as IV, 40 is represented as 10 less than 50, that is, as XL.
Let us call all these numbers that have a new basic symbol as landmark numbers.
I 1, V 5, X 10, L 50, C 100, D 500, M 1,000.
Consider the number 2367. Writing it as a sum of landmark numbers starting from 1000 such that we take as many 1000s as possible, 500s as possible, and so on, we get 2367 = 1000 + 1000 + 100 + 100 + 100 + 50 + 10 + 5 + 1 + 1.
This system seems to have evolved out of the ancient Greek number system in around the 8th century BCE in Rome, and evolved over time.

content.text:
Worked example: Write 2367 as a sum of Roman landmark numbers and then as a Roman numeral.
1. Two 1000s fit in 2367: 2367 − 2000 = 367. No 500 fits in 367.
2. Three 100s fit: 367 − 300 = 67. One 50 fits: 67 − 50 = 17.
3. One 10 fits: 17 − 10 = 7. One 5 fits: 7 − 5 = 2, which is two 1s.
4. So 2367 = 1000 + 1000 + 100 + 100 + 100 + 50 + 10 + 5 + 1 + 1.
5. Writing one symbol for each landmark, 2367 is written as MMCCCLXVII.
Answer: 2367 = 1000 + 1000 + 100 + 100 + 100 + 50 + 10 + 5 + 1 + 1, written as MMCCCLXVII

content.text:
Despite the relative efficiency of the Roman system, it doesn't lend itself to an easy performance of arithmetic operations, particularly multiplication and division.
Example: Try adding the following numbers without converting them to Hindu numerals: (a) CCXXXII + CCCCXIII
Let us find the total number of Is, Xs, and Cs, and group them starting from the largest landmark number.
Apparently, it looks like the largest landmark number is C, but note that 5 Cs (100s) make a D (500).
The efficiency of this system is due to the grouping of a given number by not just one group size, but a sequence of group sizes that we call landmark numbers.

content.text:
Worked example: Add CCXXXII and CCCCXIII without converting them to Hindu numerals.
1. Count the symbols: C's 2 + 4 = 6, X's 3 + 1 = 4, I's 2 + 3 = 5.
2. Five I's make one V.
3. Four X's are written as XL, ten less than fifty.
4. Six C's: five C's make a D, and one C is left, so DC.
5. The sum is DCXLV. Check with our numerals: 232 + 413 = 645.
Answer: DCXLV

content.text:
Worked example: Add LXXXVII and LXXVIII without converting them to Hindu numerals.
1. Count the symbols: L's 1 + 1 = 2, X's 3 + 2 = 5, V's 1 + 1 = 2, I's 2 + 3 = 5.
2. Five I's make a V, so now there are 3 V's: two of them make an X and one V stays.
3. That gives 6 X's: five make an L and one X stays, so now there are 3 L's.
4. Two L's make a C and one L stays.
5. The sum is CLXV. Check with our numerals: 87 + 78 = 165.
Answer: CLXV

concepts.concept_name: Why multiplying Roman numerals is hard

content.text:
How will you multiply two numbers given in Roman numerals, without converting them to Hindu numerals? Try to find the product of the following pairs of landmark numbers: V × L, L × D, V × D, VII × IX.
Multiply CCXXXI and MDCCCLII.
People using the Roman system made use of a calculating tool called the abacus to perform their arithmetic operations. However, only specially trained people used this tool for calculation.
While going through the number systems discussed above, it should not be understood that, historically, one system developed as an improvement over the previous system.

1. Predict first: is V × L another landmark number?
2. V × L is 5 × 50 = 250, which is CCL: not a landmark, so it needs several symbols.
3. L × D is 50 × 500 = 25000, which needs 25 M's, since no Roman symbol is bigger than M.
4. Because the landmarks grow by 5 and then by 2, their products land anywhere, so there is no simple rule for multiplying.

content.text:
Worked example: Find V × L, L × D, V × D and VII × IX in Roman numerals.
1. V × L is 5 × 50 = 250, which is 100 + 100 + 50, written as CCL.
2. L × D is 50 × 500 = 25000, which is 25 thousands, written as M repeated 25 times.
3. V × D is 5 × 500 = 2500, which is 1000 + 1000 + 500, written as MMD.
4. VII × IX is 7 × 9 = 63, which is 50 + 10 + 1 + 1 + 1, written as LXIII.
5. None of these products is a single landmark symbol, so there is no simple rule.
Answer: V × L is CCL, L × D is 25 M's, V × D is MMD and VII × IX is LXIII

content.question: Find V × L, L × D, V × D and VII × IX in Roman numerals.
steps: V × L is 5 × 50 = 250, which is 100 + 100 + 50, written as CCL.
L × D is 50 × 500 = 25000, which is 25 thousands, written as M repeated 25 times.
V × D is 5 × 500 = 2500, which is 1000 + 1000 + 500, written as MMD.
VII × IX is 7 × 9 = 63, which is 50 + 10 + 1 + 1 + 1, written as LXIII.
None of these products is a single landmark symbol, so there is no simple rule.
content.answer: V × L is CCL, L × D is 25 M's, V × D is MMD and VII × IX is LXIII

content.text:
Figure it Out (Roman numerals, question 1): Represent the following numbers in the Roman system. (i) 1222 (ii) 2999 (iii) 302 (iv) 715
1. (i) 1222 = 1000 + 100 + 100 + 10 + 10 + 1 + 1, written as MCCXXII.
2. (ii) 2999 = 1000 + 1000 + 900 + 90 + 9; 900 is CM, 90 is XC and 9 is IX, so it is written as MMCMXCIX.
3. (iii) 302 = 100 + 100 + 100 + 1 + 1, written as CCCII.
4. (iv) 715 = 500 + 100 + 100 + 10 + 5, written as DCCXV.
Answer: (i) MCCXXII (ii) MMCMXCIX (iii) CCCII (iv) DCCXV

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students write a number as a sum of the Roman landmark numbers, taking as many of the largest as possible first, and turn the sum into a Roman numeral such as MMCCCLXVII for 2367.
Students add two Roman numerals without converting them, by counting each symbol and regrouping five I's into V, five C's into D and so on, as in CCXXXII + CCCCXIII.
Students add LXXXVII and LXXVIII by counting L's, X's, V's and I's and regrouping each step into the next landmark.
Students multiply pairs of Roman landmark numbers, find that some products such as L × D have no single symbol, and explain why Roman numerals make multiplication hard.
Students write numbers in Roman numerals, list the features that make the Hindu number system more efficient than the Roman system, and refine a number system of their own.

content.text:
Figure it Out (early number systems, question 3): Identify the features of the Hindu number system that make it efficient when compared to the Roman number system.
1. Place value: in our numerals the position of a digit tells its landmark, so ten digits write every number; Roman symbols have fixed values and need new symbols for bigger numbers.
2. Zero: we have a digit 0 for an empty place; the Roman system has no symbol for zero.
3. Calculation: adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing follow simple column rules in our system, while Roman numerals make them very hard.
Answer: Place value with ten digits, a symbol for zero, and easy calculation

content.text:
Figure it Out (early number systems, question 4): Using the ideas discussed in this section, try refining the number system you might have made earlier.
1. Look at your own system: does it need one mark for every object?
2. Add a group size: give a new symbol to a group, such as five marks.
3. Add landmark numbers: give new symbols to bigger groups too, such as five groups of five.
4. Write a few numbers in the refined system and check that they are shorter than before.

concepts.concept_name: Each landmark is ten of the one before

content.text:
3.3 The Idea of a Base
I. The Egyptian Number System: We are now going to see a written number system that the Egyptians developed around 3000 BCE.
Imagine making collections of pebbles. The first landmark number is 1. Group together 10 collections of the previous landmark number (1). Its size is the second landmark number which is 10. Group together 10 collections of the previous landmark number (10). Its size is the third landmark number which is 10 × 10 = 100, and so on.
Each landmark number is 10 times the previous one. Since 1 is the first landmark number, they are all powers of 10.
As in the case of Roman numbers, a given number is counted in groups of the landmark numbers, starting from the largest landmark number less than the given number.
For example 324 which equals 100 + 100 + 100 + 10 + 10 + 4 is written as three coils, two heels and four strokes.

content.text:
1. Predict first: if each new landmark is ten of the last, what comes after 1, 10 and 100?
2. Ten 1s make 10, ten 10s make 100, ten 100s make 1000: every landmark is a power of 10.
3. The Egyptians drew a stroke for 1, a heel for 10, a coil for 100, a lotus for 1000, and so on up to 10000000.
4. To write a number, take as many of the largest landmark as fit, then the next, and draw that many symbols.

content.text:
Worked example: Write 2153 in Egyptian numerals.
1. The largest landmark that fits is 1000: two of them, 2153 − 2000 = 153.
2. One 100 fits: 153 − 100 = 53.
3. Five 10s fit: 53 − 50 = 3, which is three 1s.
4. So 2153 = 1000 + 1000 + 100 + 10 + 10 + 10 + 10 + 10 + 1 + 1 + 1.
5. It is written as 2 lotuses, 1 coil, 5 heels and 3 strokes.
Answer: 2 lotuses, 1 coil, 5 heels and 3 strokes

content.text:
Worked example: An Egyptian numeral shows 3 lotuses, 4 heels and 6 strokes. What number is it?
1. 3 lotuses: 1000 + 1000 + 1000 = 3000.
2. No coils, so no hundreds.
3. 4 heels: 10 + 10 + 10 + 10 = 40. 6 strokes: 6.
4. Total: 3000 + 40 + 6 = 3046.
Answer: 3046

content.text:
Figure it Out (Egyptian numerals, question 1): Represent the following numbers in the Egyptian system: 10458, 1023, 2660, 784, 1111, 70707.
1. 10458 = 10000 + 400 + 50 + 8: 1 finger, 4 coils, 5 heels and 8 strokes.
2. 1023 = 1000 + 20 + 3: 1 lotus, 2 heels and 3 strokes. 2660 = 2000 + 600 + 60: 2 lotuses, 6 coils and 6 heels.
3. 784 = 700 + 80 + 4: 7 coils, 8 heels and 4 strokes. 1111 = 1000 + 100 + 10 + 1: one lotus, one coil, one heel and one stroke.
4. 70707 = 70000 + 700 + 7: 7 fingers, 7 coils and 7 strokes.
Answer: 10458: 1 finger, 4 coils, 5 heels, 8 strokes; 1023: 1 lotus, 2 heels, 3 strokes; 2660: 2 lotuses, 6 coils, 6 heels; 784: 7 coils, 8 heels, 4 strokes; 1111: one of each of lotus, coil, heel, stroke; 70707: 7 fingers, 7 coils, 7 strokes

media.description: A number is written in the Egyptian system by taking the biggest landmark that fits, as many times as it fits, and then moving down. The video does this for 2153 with the stroke, heel, coil and lotus. Keeko's doubt is that fifteen heels can stand in place of a coil.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: take the biggest landmark that fits, as many times as it fits, then move to the next one down. Each Egyptian landmark is ten times the one before it. Watch for students who write ten or more of the same symbol.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students build the Egyptian landmarks 1, 10, 100, 1000 and onwards by grouping 10 of each into the next, and write a number such as 2153 as lotuses, coils, heels and strokes.

content.text:
Figure it Out (Egyptian numerals, question 2): What numbers do these numerals stand for? (i) 2 coils, 7 heels and 6 strokes (ii) 4 lotuses, 3 coils, 2 heels and 2 strokes
1. (i) 2 coils make 200, 7 heels make 70 and 6 strokes make 6.
2. 200 + 70 + 6 = 276.
3. (ii) 4 lotuses make 4000, 3 coils make 300, 2 heels make 20 and 2 strokes make 2.
4. 4000 + 300 + 20 + 2 = 4322.
Answer: (i) 276 (ii) 4322

content.text:
II. Variations on the Egyptian System and the Notion of Base
Instead of grouping together 10 collections of size equal to the previous landmark number (as in the case of the Egyptian system), can we get a number system by grouping together 5 collections of size equal to the previous landmark number? Can this 5 be replaced by any positive integer?
Group together 5 collections of size equal to the previous landmark number (1). Its size is the second landmark number which is 5.
Thus, we have a new number system where each landmark number is 5 times the previous one. Since 1 is the first landmark number, they are all powers of 5.
Express the number 143 in this new system. Let us start grouping, starting with the size 5³ = 125, as this is the largest landmark number smaller than 143. We get 143 = 125 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 1 + 1 + 1.

content.text:
Worked example: Write 89 in the base-5 system with triangle 1, square 5, hexagon 25 and circle 125.
1. 125 is bigger than 89, so start with 25: three 25s fit, 89 − 75 = 14.
2. Two 5s fit in 14: 14 − 10 = 4, which is four 1s.
3. So 89 = 25 + 25 + 25 + 5 + 5 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1.
4. It is written as 3 hexagons, 2 squares and 4 triangles.
Answer: 3 hexagons, 2 squares and 4 triangles

concepts.concept_name: Base n: the landmarks are the powers of n

content.text:
Number systems having landmark numbers in which the (a) first landmark number is 1, and (b) every next landmark number is obtained by multiplying the current landmark number by some fixed number n is said to be a base-n number system.
The Egyptian number system is a base-10 system, and the number system that we created is a base-5 system. A base-10 number system is also called a decimal number system.
The landmark numbers of a base-n number system are the powers of n starting from 1, n, n², n³, ...

4. Any counting number bigger than 1 can be a base.

content.text:
Worked example: Find the first five landmark numbers of a base-3 system and write 50 as a sum of them.
1. Start at 1 and multiply by 3: 1, 3, 9, 27, 81.
2. 81 is bigger than 50, so start with 27: one fits, 50 − 27 = 23.
3. Two 9s fit in 23: 23 − 18 = 5. One 3 fits: 5 − 3 = 2, which is two 1s.
4. So 50 = 27 + 9 + 9 + 3 + 1 + 1.
Answer: Landmarks 1, 3, 9, 27, 81; 50 = 27 + 9 + 9 + 3 + 1 + 1

Figure it Out (base-n systems, question 1): Write the following numbers in the above base-5 system using the symbols in Table 2: 15, 50, 137, 293, 651.
1. 15 = 5 + 5 + 5: 3 squares. 50 = 25 + 25: 2 hexagons.
2. 137 = 125 + 5 + 5 + 1 + 1: 1 circle, 2 squares and 2 triangles.
3. 293 = 125 + 125 + 25 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 1 + 1 + 1: 2 circles, 1 hexagon, 3 squares and 3 triangles.
4. 651 = 625 + 25 + 1: 1 wave, 1 hexagon and 1 triangle.
Answer: 15: 3 squares; 50: 2 hexagons; 137: 1 circle, 2 squares, 2 triangles; 293: 2 circles, 1 hexagon, 3 squares, 3 triangles; 651: 1 wave, 1 hexagon, 1 triangle

content.text:
Figure it Out (base-n systems, question 2): Is there a number that cannot be represented in our base-5 system above? Why or why not?
1. Every counting number can be grouped into powers of 5, using each symbol at most 4 times.
2. As numbers grow, we only need more landmark symbols, which can always be invented.
3. But 0 is the number of objects in an empty collection, and there is no symbol to draw for it.
4. So 0 cannot be represented.
Answer: Yes: 0 cannot be represented, because the system has no symbol for it

content.text:
Figure it Out (base-n systems, question 3): Compute the landmark numbers of a base-7 system. In general, what are the landmark numbers of a base-n system?
1. Start at 1 and multiply by 7 each time: 1, 7, 7 × 7 = 49, 49 × 7 = 343, 343 × 7 = 2401.
2. In general, start at 1 and multiply by n each time.
3. So the landmarks of base n are 1, n, n², n³, and so on, the powers of n.
Answer: Base 7: 1, 7, 49, 343, 2401, ...; base n: 1, n, n², n³, ..., the powers of n

content.text:
Figure it Out (bases and their limits, question 1): Can there be a number whose representation in Egyptian numerals has one of the symbols occurring 10 or more times? Why not?
1. Every Egyptian landmark is 10 times the one before.
2. If a symbol appeared 10 times, those 10 symbols would make exactly one symbol of the next landmark.
3. Grouping always takes as many of the larger landmark as possible, so the 10 would be regrouped.
4. So no symbol is ever written 10 or more times.
Answer: No: 10 of any symbol make one of the next landmark, so they are always regrouped

content.text:
Figure it Out (bases and their limits, question 2): Create your own number system of base 4, and represent numbers from 1 to 16.
1. Landmarks of base 4: 1, 4, 16. Give them symbols, for example a dot for 1, a stick for 4 and a square for 16.
2. 1, 2, 3 are 1, 2, 3 dots; 4 is a stick; 5, 6, 7 are a stick and 1, 2, 3 dots.
3. 8 is 2 sticks; 9, 10, 11 add 1, 2, 3 dots; 12 is 3 sticks; 13, 14, 15 add 1, 2, 3 dots.
4. 16 is one square, since four sticks make the next landmark.
Answer: Landmarks 1, 4, 16; for example 7 is a stick and 3 dots, 12 is 3 sticks, 16 is one square

2. 1, 2, 3 are 1, 2, 3 dots; 4 is a stick; 5, 6, 7 are a stick and 1, 2, 3 dots.
3. 8 is 2 sticks; 9, 10, 11 add 1, 2, 3 dots; 12 is 3 sticks; 13, 14, 15 add 1, 2, 3 dots.
4. 16 is one square, since four sticks make the next landmark.
Answer: Landmarks 1, 4, 16; for example 7 is a stick and 3 dots, 12 is 3 sticks, 16 is one square

segments.segment_name: Adding and Multiplying with a Base

content.text:
Advantages of a Base-n System
What is the advantage of having landmark numbers that are all the powers of a number? To understand this, let us perform some arithmetic operations using them.
Let us find the total number of strokes and heels and group them starting from the largest possible landmark number. It has a total of 15 heels and 15 strokes.
Since 10 heels gives the next landmark number, a coil, the sum can be regrouped.
I see a similarity in the method of adding numbers in the Egyptian and the Hindu system!
Contrast the addition done in a base-n number system with that done in the Roman system. In the Roman system, the grouping and rearranging has to be done carefully as it is not always by the same size that each landmark number has to be grouped to get the next one.

content.text:
1. Predict first: when you add 87 and 78 in Egyptian numerals, will you need a coil?
2. Put all the symbols together and count each kind.
3. Every 10 strokes become 1 heel, every 10 heels become 1 coil: the same rule at every step.
4. This is exactly the carrying we do when adding in columns; in Roman numerals the group size keeps changing.

content.text:
Worked example: Add 8 heels and 7 strokes to 7 heels and 8 strokes in Egyptian numerals.
1. Count each kind: heels 8 + 7 = 15, strokes 7 + 8 = 15.
2. Ten strokes make one heel: 15 strokes become 1 heel and 5 strokes, so there are now 16 heels.
3. Ten heels make one coil: 16 heels become 1 coil and 6 heels.
4. The sum is 1 coil, 6 heels and 5 strokes, which is 165. Check: 87 + 78 = 165.
Answer: 1 coil, 6 heels and 5 strokes, which is 165

concepts.concept_name: A landmark times a landmark is a landmark

content.text:
How to multiply two numbers in Egyptian numerals? Let us first consider the product of two landmark numbers.
What is any landmark number multiplied by a heel (that is 10)?
Each landmark number is a power of 10 and so multiplying it with 10 increases the power by 1, which is the next landmark number.
Thus, the product of any two landmark numbers is another landmark number!
Does this property hold true in the base-5 system that we created? Does this hold for any number system with a base?

content.text:
1. Predict first: is 100 × 1000 one Egyptian symbol or many?
2. Multiplying a landmark by 10 gives the next landmark: 100 × 10 = 1000, a coil becomes a lotus.
3. Multiplying by 100 moves two landmarks up: 1000 × 100 = 100000, a lotus becomes a tadpole.
4. Landmarks are powers of the base, and a power times a power is a power, so this holds in every base, unlike in Roman numerals.

content.text:
Worked example: Find 100 × 10, 1000 × 100 and 100 × 1000 in Egyptian numerals, and check 25 × 125 in base 5.
1. 100 × 10 = 1000: a coil times a heel is a lotus.
2. 1000 × 100 = 100000: a lotus times a coil is a tadpole.
3. 100 × 1000 = 100000: a coil times a lotus is also a tadpole.
4. In base 5, a hexagon times a circle: 25 × 125 = 3125, which is the arrow, another landmark.
5. In each case the product is a single landmark symbol.
Answer: A lotus, a tadpole, a tadpole, and in base 5 an arrow; each product is a landmark

content.text:
What can we conclude about the product of a number and a heel (10), in the Egyptian system?
Will the distributive property hold here? For the same reason that it holds for (a + b) × n, it also holds when one of the numbers has more than 2 terms. For example, (a + b + c) × n = an + bn + cn.
What would be a simple rule to multiply a number with a heel?
When the landmark numbers are powers of a number, then their product is another landmark number. This fact simplifies the process of multiplication.
Thus, a number system whose landmark numbers are powers of a number, i.e., a number system with a base, is efficient not only in number representation but also in its utility in carrying out arithmetic operations.

content.text:
1. Predict first: what happens to each symbol of 121 when the number is multiplied by 10?
2. Split the number into its symbols and multiply each one by 10: the distributive property.
3. Each symbol becomes the next landmark: a stroke becomes a heel, a heel a coil, a coil a lotus.
4. So the rule is: to multiply by 10, move every symbol up one landmark.

content.text:
Worked example: Multiply 121 (1 coil, 2 heels, 1 stroke) by 10, then use the rule to find 522 × 10.
1. 121 = 100 + 10 + 10 + 1, so 121 × 10 = (100 + 10 + 10 + 1) × 10.
2. By the distributive property: 100 × 10 + 10 × 10 + 10 × 10 + 1 × 10 = 1000 + 100 + 100 + 10.
3. So 121 × 10 = 1210: 1 lotus, 2 coils and 1 heel; every symbol moved up one landmark.
4. 522 is 5 coils, 2 heels and 2 strokes; moving each up gives 5 lotuses, 2 coils and 2 heels, so 522 × 10 = 5220.
Answer: 121 × 10 is 1210 (1 lotus, 2 coils, 1 heel) and 522 × 10 is 5220

content.text:
Abacus that Makes Use of the Decimal System
In around the 11th century, even the people still using the Roman numerals started using a calculating device, the abacus, constructed using a decimal system.
Starting from the line that stood for 1, each successive line stood for a successive power of 10.
The presence of a counter above a line contributed a value of 5.
For example let us take the number 3426. It can be grouped as 3426 = 1000 + 1000 + 1000 + 100 + 100 + 100 + 100 + 10 + 10 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1.
Let us consider a simple addition problem: 2907 + 43. The two numbers were taken on either side of the vertical partition.
Hint: In this problem, the 7 ones and the 3 ones together make 10 ones which contributes a counter to the line representing 10s.

content.text:
Worked example: Add 2907 and 43 on the counting board.
1. 2907 has 2 counters on the thousands line, 9 on the hundreds line (one above it for 5 and 4 on it), none for tens and 7 for ones; 43 has 4 tens and 3 ones.
2. Bring the ones together: 7 + 3 = 10 ones, which become 1 counter on the tens line.
3. Tens: 4 + 1 = 5, shown by one counter above the tens line.
4. Hundreds stay 9 and thousands stay 2, so the board shows 2950.
Answer: 2950

content.text:
Figure it Out (adding with landmarks, question 1): Add the following Egyptian numerals: (i) 9 lotuses, 6 coils and 8 strokes + 5 coils and 7 strokes (ii) 1 lotus and 8 heels + 4 heels and 6 strokes
1. (i) Strokes 8 + 7 = 15: 1 heel and 5 strokes. Coils 6 + 5 = 11: 1 lotus and 1 coil.
2. Lotuses 9 + 1 = 10: 1 finger. The sum is 1 finger, 1 coil, 1 heel and 5 strokes, which is 10115. Check: 9608 + 507 = 10115.
3. (ii) Strokes: 6. Heels 8 + 4 = 12: 1 coil and 2 heels.
4. The sum is 1 lotus, 1 coil, 2 heels and 6 strokes, which is 1126. Check: 1080 + 46 = 1126.
Answer: (i) 1 finger, 1 coil, 1 heel, 5 strokes, which is 10115 (ii) 1 lotus, 1 coil, 2 heels, 6 strokes, which is 1126

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students add two Egyptian numerals by counting each symbol and regrouping every 10 strokes into a heel and every 10 heels into a coil, as in 87 + 78.
Students multiply Egyptian landmark numbers by 10 and by 100, find that each product is another landmark, check the same property in base 5, and explain why it holds in every base.
Students multiply an Egyptian numeral by 10 with the distributive property, moving every symbol up one landmark, as in 121 × 10, and state the rule for multiplying by the base.
Students show a number on a counting board with lines for powers of 10 and a counter above a line for 5, and add 2907 and 43 by bringing counters together and carrying 10 ones to the tens line.
Students add Egyptian numerals and base-5 numerals by regrouping, and give a rule for multiplying a base-5 numeral by 5.

content.text:
Figure it Out (adding with landmarks, question 2): Add the following numerals that are in the base-5 system that we created: (1 circle, 2 hexagons, 1 square, 2 triangles) + (3 circles, 1 hexagon, 2 squares, 2 triangles). Remember that in this system, 5 times a landmark number gives the next one!
1. Count each kind: circles 1 + 3 = 4, hexagons 2 + 1 = 3, squares 1 + 2 = 3, triangles 2 + 2 = 4.
2. No kind reaches 5, so nothing needs to be regrouped.
3. The sum is 4 circles, 3 hexagons, 3 squares and 4 triangles.
4. Check in our numerals: 182 + 412 = 594, and 500 + 75 + 15 + 4 = 594.
Answer: 4 circles, 3 hexagons, 3 squares and 4 triangles, which is 594

content.text:
Figure it Out (bases and their limits, question 3): Give a simple rule to multiply a given number by 5 in the base-5 system that we created.
1. Each landmark times 5 is the next landmark: 1 × 5 = 5, 5 × 5 = 25, 25 × 5 = 125.
2. By the distributive property, multiply every symbol of the number by 5.
3. So every triangle becomes a square, every square a hexagon, every hexagon a circle, and so on.
4. Rule: replace each symbol by the symbol of the next landmark.
Answer: Replace every symbol by the symbol of the next landmark

content.text:
III. Shortcomings of the Egyptian System
If larger and larger numbers needed to be represented, then there was a need for inventing an unending sequence of symbols for higher and higher powers of 10.
3.4 Place Value Representation. I. The Mesopotamian Number System
In later times, it became a base-60 system, also called the sexagesimal system, with a very efficient number representation.
The influence of the Mesopotamian sexagesimal system, also known as the Babylonian number system, can be seen even now in our units of time measurements: 1 hour is 60 minutes and 1 minute is 60 seconds.
Note that we have actually used Indian numerals in creating these symbols.
Example: Let us represent the number 640 in this system. Grouping it into landmark numbers, we see that 640 = (10) × 60 + 40.
Example: Let us try another number, 7530. 7530 = (2) × 3600 + (5) × 60 + 30.

content.text:
Worked example: Group 4000 into powers of 60 and say how it is written in base 60 with our own symbols.
1. The landmarks are 1, 60 and 3600; 216000 is far too big.
2. One 3600 fits in 4000: 4000 − 3600 = 400.
3. Six 60s fit in 400: 6 × 60 = 360, and 400 − 360 = 40.
4. So 4000 = (1) × 3600 + (6) × 60 + 40.
5. It is written as 1 with the 3600 symbol, 6 with the 60 symbol, and 40.
Answer: 4000 = (1) × 3600 + (6) × 60 + 40

content.text:
Note that when a number is grouped into powers of 60 for its representation, no power of 60 can occur 60 or more times. If this happens, then 60 of them can be grouped to form the next power of 60.
(1) × 3600 + (70) × 60 + 2 = (1) × 3600 + (60 + 10) × 60 + 2 = (2) × 3600 + (10) × 60 + 2.
Therefore, any number can be represented using the numerals from 1 to 59, along with the numerals for landmark numbers.

4. Every count then lies from 1 to 59.

content.text:
Worked example: Regroup (2) × 3600 + (75) × 60 + 10 so that no count is 60 or more.
1. 75 sixties is 60 sixties and 15 sixties.
2. 60 sixties make one 3600, so the 3600s go from 2 to 3.
3. So (2) × 3600 + (75) × 60 + 10 = (3) × 3600 + (15) × 60 + 10.
4. Both are 11710: 7200 + 4500 + 10 and 10800 + 900 + 10.
Answer: (3) × 3600 + (15) × 60 + 10, which is 11710

content.text:
Now, what if we make the representation even more compact by dropping the symbols for the different powers of 60 altogether?
This is exactly what the Mesopotamians did! In their numeral, the rightmost set of symbols showed the number of 1s, the set of symbols to its left showed the number of 60s, the next showed the number of 3600s and so on. Whenever there was no occurrence of a power of 60, a blank space was given in that position.
Such a number system (having a base) that makes use of the position of each symbol in determining the landmark number that it is associated with is called a positional number system or a place value system.
This idea of place value marks the highest point in the history of evolution of number systems.

4. A system with a base where position gives the landmark is a place value system.

content.text:
Worked example: Write 3725 in the Mesopotamian place value system, using our numerals for each place.
1. One 3600 fits: 3725 − 3600 = 125.
2. Two 60s fit in 125: 125 − 120 = 5.
3. So 3725 = (1) × 3600 + (2) × 60 + 5.
4. Dropping the landmark symbols, it is written 1 | 2 | 5: 1 in the 3600s place, 2 in the 60s place, 5 in the 1s place.
Answer: 1 | 2 | 5, from 3725 = (1) × 3600 + (2) × 60 + 5

content.text:
Figure it Out (Mesopotamian numerals, question 1): Represent the following numbers in the Mesopotamian system: (i) 63 (ii) 132 (iii) 200 (iv) 60 (v) 3605
1. (i) 63 = (1) × 60 + 3, written 1 | 3. (ii) 132 = (2) × 60 + 12, written 2 | 12.
2. (iii) 200 = (3) × 60 + 20, written 3 | 20.
3. (iv) 60 = (1) × 60, so the 1s place is empty: written 1 followed by a blank.
4. (v) 3605 = (1) × 3600 + 5, so the 60s place is empty: written 1 | blank | 5.
Answer: (i) 1 | 3 (ii) 2 | 12 (iii) 3 | 20 (iv) 1 | blank (v) 1 | blank | 5

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students explain why a base with a symbol for every landmark needs endless symbols, group a number such as 4000 into powers of 60, and write it with the numerals 1 to 59 and the landmark symbols.
Students regroup a base-60 grouping in which a power of 60 occurs 60 or more times, so that every count is from 1 to 59.
Students drop the landmark symbols and read a base-60 numeral by position, the rightmost group counting 1s, the next 60s and the next 3600s, and define a place value system.
Students write numbers in the Mesopotamian place value system, including numbers with an empty place.

content.text:
The Mesopotamian system however cannot be considered a fully developed place value system. It has certain defects that lead to confusion while reading a number.
Look at the representation of 60. What will be the representation for 3,600?
Because of the ambiguity in finding which symbols correspond to which powers of 60, the same numeral can be read in different ways.
To address the issue arising out of blank spaces, the later Mesopotamians used a brilliant idea of assigning a 'placeholder' symbol to denote a blank space. This is like the 0 (zero) we use in our system.
The placeholder symbol was primarily used in the middle of numbers and not at the end; so they would not use it to represent a number like (what we would write as) 3600.

Worked example: A Mesopotamian numeral shows 2 and then 5, with a gap between them that might hide an empty place. What two numbers could it be?
1. If there is no empty place, 2 counts 60s and 5 counts 1s: 2 × 60 + 5 = 125.
2. If an empty 60s place is hidden in the gap, 2 counts 3600s: 2 × 3600 + 5 = 7205.
3. The same marks give 125 or 7205.
4. A placeholder written in the empty place would remove the doubt.
Answer: 125 or 7205; only a placeholder for the empty place settles it

concepts.concept_name: The Mayan system and its shell

content.text:
II. The Mayan Number System
In Central America, there flourished a civilisation known as the Mayan civilisation that made great intellectual and cultural progress between the 3rd and 10th centuries CE. Among their intellectual achievements stands their place value system designed independently of those in Asia. They also made use of a placeholder symbol, for the modern-day '0', that looked like a seashell.
Why was their third landmark number 360 rather than 400? Some scholars feel that this might have something to do with their calendars.
They used a dot for 1, and a bar for 5. These were used to denote numbers from 1 to 19.
The symbols associated with different landmark numbers were written one below the other with the lowermost set of symbols corresponding to the number of 1s, the set above corresponding to the number of 20s, the set above to the number of 360s and so on.
Because the Mayan system is not an actual base-20 system, it lacks the advantages that a system with a base has for computations.
A curious fact is that we can still find the use of base-20 in the number names of some European languages.

content.text:
Worked example: A Mayan numeral shows, from top to bottom, two dots, then three dots, then one bar. What number is it?
1. Read from the bottom: the lowest place counts 1s, the next 20s, the top 360s.
2. The bottom is one bar, which is 5. The middle is three dots, which is 3. The top is two dots, which is 2.
3. So the number is 2 × 360 + 3 × 20 + 5.
4. 2 × 360 + 3 × 20 + 5 = 785.
Answer: 785

1. 77 = 3 × 20 + 17: three dots over three bars and two dots.

4. 721 = 2 × 360 + 0 × 20 + 1: two dots, a shell, one dot.

content.text:
III. The Chinese Number System
The Chinese used two number systems: a written system for recording quantities, and a system making use of rods for performing computations. The numerals in the rod-based number system are called rod numerals.
It was a decimal system (base-10).
Note: The zongs represent units, hundreds, tens of thousands, etc., and the hengs tens, thousands, hundreds of thousands, etc.
(2) × 10³ + (6) × 10² + (3) × 10 + (4) × 1 = 2634
Like the Mesopotamians, the rod numerals used a blank space to indicate the skipping of a place value. However, because of the slightly more uniform sizes of the symbols for one through nine, the blank spaces were easier to locate than in the Mesopotamian system.
The Chinese system, with a symbol for zero, would be a fully developed place value system.

4. (5) × 10³ + (0) × 10² + (7) × 10 + (2) × 1 = 5072.
Answer: 5 heng, a blank, 7 heng, 2 zong, which is 5072

content.text:
Figure it Out (place value, question 1): Why do you think the Chinese alternated between the Zong and Heng symbols? If only the Zong symbols were to be used, how would 41 be represented? Could this numeral be interpreted in any other way if there is no significant space between two successive positions?
1. Alternating shapes shows where one place ends and the next begins.
2. With zongs only, 41 is four vertical rods for the tens and one vertical rod for the units: 5 rods in a row.
3. Without a clear gap, 5 rods could be read as 5, as 2 then 3 (23), as 3 then 2 (32), or as 1, 2, 2 (122).
4. So alternating zong and heng keeps neighbouring places apart.
Answer: To keep neighbouring places apart; with zongs only 41 is 4 rods and 1 rod, which could also be read as 5, 23, 32 or 122

media.title: Zero Placeholder Breaker
media.context: CBSE Class 8, NCERT Ganita Prakash Chapter 3 'A Story of Numbers', place value and the invention of zero. It is read straight after positional place value, while the columns are still fresh, and before the chapter's climax that finitely many symbols plus position plus zero can write every number. This is a history-of-notation chapter, not a remedial place-value one: a Class 8 student has done place value since Class 2, and the felt difficulty is structural, why a positional system had to invent this symbol, so every caption is pitched at why the notation must work this way and never at 'remember your place values'. Zero is taught here as a PLACEHOLDER only; its arithmetic as a number (Brahmagupta's 0 + n = n) belongs to the same chapter but not to this mount.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's board, the correct board, and the number line that explains the gap.
whatYouLearned: An empty column collapses and every digit to its left loses a place
A zero holds a place open and adds nothing to the total
Trailing zeros are needed for the same reason internal ones are
A single digit number needs no zero, so the rule is about places and not about numbers

overview.goal: The student shows what goes wrong when a place is left empty instead of holding a zero, and states the rule for when a zero is needed.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A row of labelled place value columns with a digit tile tray beneath and a short number line under the readout. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class leaves the tens column empty and expects the board to still read the number they meant, and the board is asked to say what it actually reads.
overview.concept: In a positional system the place of a digit carries its value, so every place between the first digit and the last must be accounted for. Leaving a column empty does not record an absence, it removes the column, and the digits to its left slide down. A zero is the symbol that holds a place open without adding anything to the total.
overview.purpose: The student shows what goes wrong when a place is left empty instead of holding a zero, and states the rule for when a zero is needed.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Board across the upper main panel, readout directly beneath, number line under that. On a 390 px frame the column labels abbreviate but never disappear, and every tile keeps a 44 px hit target. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not show the readout while a prediction is still open, and never pad an empty column with a zero the student did not place. Padding would hide the whole phenomenon.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. The value of a digit is the digit times the power of ten for its column, and the column is fixed by counting places from the right. If a place is simply left out, everything to its left is counted from one place further right and so is worth ten times less. The zero contributes nothing to the sum but everything to the counting, which is why it is a placeholder rather than a quantity here. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): The zero rule is not a habit to apply everywhere; a number with no internal place needs none. Breaks: Over applying the placeholder rule so that every number is thought to need a zero. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): Trailing zeros hold places open exactly as internal ones do, so the rule is not about the middle. Breaks: Believing zeros only matter when they sit between other digits. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): A zero earns its place only when it separates digits, which is what makes leading and internal zeros different. Breaks: Zero read as nothing, so its position is treated as making no difference either way. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): Each empty column costs its own place, so a board with two gaps has more than one wrong repair. Breaks: Treating a collapsed reading as a near miss that one correction will fix. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): A rule is only accepted once it survives the case that breaks the over general one and the case that breaks the under general one. Breaks: Place value seen as digit order without column meaning, so a rule about position is never tested.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with 3 in hundreds and 5 in ones, the tens column empty and the readout HIDDEN, and asks what number will be read. Beat 2 reveals the collapse to 35 and plots both numbers on a line so the size difference is visible. Beat 3 drops the zero tile into the tens column and the board re anchors to 305. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with placeTile, removeTile, readAloud and say. No drag: the agent cannot drag a tile with finite calls.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the board with one column deliberately empty, no zero tiles in the tray, and the readout HIDDEN, and ask the class what number the board will be read as. Commit the class number on the prediction pad. Targets the seated tiles and the empty column, read from the tool's own list of empty columns. Never show the readout before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Reveal the reading and plot the intended value and the actual value on the same line, then point at the span between them. Targets the readout, the two markers and the labelled span. Read both values from the tool's own readouts and say how many times smaller the actual value is. Call 3. Turn on the zero tile supply and seat a zero in the empty column, then point at each column as it re anchors. Targets the zero tile, the repaired column and the restored readout. Say what the zero added to the total, which is nothing, and what it added to the reading.

hunts: TENFOLD DROP: build a board, take one column out, and check that the reading lost exactly one place.
TWO GAPS: leave two columns empty and find every wrong number one repair can still give.
TRAILING TEST: build a number ending in zeros and remove them one at a time, naming what each removal costs.
RULE HUNT: write your own rule for when a zero is needed, then run it on 5000 and on 5.

observationsAndConclusions.why: Every digit to the left of the gap loses a place, so each of them is worth one tenth of what it was
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Removing one tile from the middle changes the reading by far more than that tile was worth
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The damage a missing place does grows with how many digits sit to its left

observationsAndConclusions.why: The zero adds nothing to the total and restores the counting of the places
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Seating a zero moves no other tile and changes the reading completely
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A placeholder is not a quantity, it is a position keeper

observationsAndConclusions.why: A zero is required wherever a place still has to be counted, and a single digit number has no such place
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The single digit case needs no zero and the trailing zero case needs every one of them
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A rule tested only in the middle of a number is not yet a rule

media.description: A row of place-value columns is drawn right to left with the ones at the right, each column headed by its power of ten and footed by its value and its name. A digit tile seats in a column; a column left empty is drawn as a visibly hollow slot and is NEVER padded with a zero the student did not place. Underneath, a reading strip states what the board ACTUALLY says: the surviving digits travel out of their columns and close up into a shorter numeral over 260 ms, so the loss of a place is seen as a movement rather than reported as a value. Beside it the chapter's own expanded form is written with the zero term present (3 × 10² + 0 × 10¹ + 5 × 10⁰ = 305), and beneath it one number line carries both the intended value and the collapsed one on a single unit from a single origin, with the shortfall labelled across the span between them, so the error has a size rather than a name. Concept walks three beats, the collapse, why a lost place costs a tenth, and the repair. Learn walks the five reviewed checkpoints, each building its board from that checkpoint's own numbers and opening with its answer already on screen. Practice serves six items drawn from a thirty item pool on a difficulty ladder, every item rendering the board its own question describes, with the reading and the shortfall masked until the answer is in. Free Play unlocks the tray, the zero tile supply, the column count and a rule tester that runs any stated rule on 5000 and on 5 and names the case that breaks it.

modes.ai: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with 3 in hundreds and 5 in ones, the tens column empty and the readout HIDDEN, and asks what number will be read. Beat 2 reveals the collapse to 35 and plots both numbers on a line so the size difference is visible. Beat 3 drops the zero tile into the tens column and the board re anchors to 305. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with placeTile, removeTile, readAloud and say. No drag: the agent cannot drag a tile with finite calls.
modes.learn: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets the target number from its own digits, shows the question, then reveals the board, the collapse or the repair and the answer together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
modes.normal: Free Play, student operated. The student places and removes any digit tile, turns the zero tile supply on and off, and reads any board aloud in text. Nothing is scored and nothing is mandatory.
modes.practice: Practice, student operated. The bank from props.questions, one item at a time, each rendering its own board. Build a spoken or written number, say which columns need a zero, or read what a gappy board actually says. Scored, with a star finish and a Review phase that walks every item showing the student's board, the correct board and the number line that settles it.

theme.premise: A class leaves the tens column empty and expects the board to still read the number they meant, and the board is asked to say what it actually reads
theme.setting: A row of labelled place value columns with a digit tile tray beneath and a short number line under the readout
theme.visualStyle: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration
theme.studentPalette: The warmer accent of the same family, with the score and the Finish button carrying it
theme.teacherPalette: The cool indigo accent, low chrome, high contrast, so a projected board stays readable

practice.rating: all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1, never 0
practice.review: The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's board, the correct board, and the number line that explains the gap.

whatYouLearned: An empty column collapses and every digit to its left loses a place
A zero holds a place open and adds nothing to the total
Trailing zeros are needed for the same reason internal ones are
A single digit number needs no zero, so the rule is about places and not about numbers

scenes.interaction: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.
scenes.valuesShown: Every readout stays live, so the invariants keep being computed while the student explores

concept.notation: A place value board is written as a row of columns. An empty column is not the same as a column holding 0; the first collapses and the second holds.
concept.statement: In a positional system the place of a digit carries its value, so every place between the first digit and the last must be accounted for. Leaving a column empty does not record an absence, it removes the column, and the digits to its left slide down. A zero is the symbol that holds a place open without adding anything to the total.
prerequisites: positional place value and expanded form
reading a number from its columns
misconceptions: Zero read as nothing, so it is thought safe to omit.
Place value seen as digit order without column meaning, so 305 and 35 are expected to differ only in length.
concept.why_it_is_true: The value of a digit is the digit times the power of ten for its column, and the column is fixed by counting places from the right. If a place is simply left out, everything to its left is counted from one place further right and so is worth ten times less. The zero contributes nothing to the sum but everything to the counting, which is why it is a placeholder rather than a quantity here.
worked_numbers: 3 in hundreds and 5 in ones with the tens left empty reads as 35, not 305.
Placing the zero tile in tens restores 305, and the 3 goes back to being worth 300.
3005 needs two internal zeros, and leaving either out gives 305 or 350 rather than a near miss.

testRuleOutcomes.every number needs a zero somewhere: fails on the single digit number, which needs none
testRuleOutcomes.a zero is needed only between two digits: fails on a number ending in zeros, where dropping a trailing zero divides the value by ten
testRuleOutcomes.a zero is never needed at the end of a n: fails on the number ending in zeros, which loses a place at once
testRuleOutcomes.a zero is needed at every empty place th: holds on the number ending in zeros and on the single digit number

placeTileOutcomes.ones: the tile seats in the rightmost column and the reading is rebuilt from the whole board
placeTileOutcomes.tens: the tile seats one place left of the ones column; seating a zero here is the repair the beat is about
placeTileOutcomes.hundreds: the tile seats two places left of the ones column and is worth a hundred times its face value
placeTileOutcomes.thousands: the tile seats three places left of the ones column and is worth a thousand times its face value

setZeroSupplyOutcomes.on: zero tiles appear in the tray and none of them is placed for the student
setZeroSupplyOutcomes.off: the tray offers the digits one to nine only, which is the state the collapse is demonstrated in

answer_key.worked: An empty column collapses and the digits to its left lose a place each. A zero holds the place open and adds nothing to the total.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn board: the number the board actually reads, the required zero positions for a target, or the difference between the intended and the collapsed value.
answer_key.precision: The board is an array of digit or null values and the rendered number is derived from it, so the collapse is a consequence rather than a special case. Integer arithmetic only.
answer_key.ground_truth: readBoard(cells) = the digit string formed by dropping every null, then read as an integer. requiredZeros(target) = the indices where the target's digit string holds a 0 between its first and last digit. intended(cells) = the value the student meant, computed from the columns they used.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Every trailing zero is required and the tool says so, because dropping one divides the number by ten. This is the case that stops the rule being read as 'zeros only matter in the middle'.

edge_cases.case: A single digit number, as in 5
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: No zero is needed anywhere, and the tool says so explicitly. This is the case that stops the rule being over applied to every number.
It holds no place open and is dropped from the value, and the tool explains the difference from an internal zero rather than accepting or refusing it silently.
Both are required and omitting either gives a different wrong number. The tool shows both wrong readings rather than only the nearest one.
The readout is empty and the tool says there is no number yet. It never renders a 0 that the student did not place.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later.
hostProps.device: mobile / web / smartboard. Lay out for the 390 px frame first.
hostProps.questions: TOP LEVEL. The Practice bank the platform drew for this concept, from question_bank_v2 where delivery_mode = 'Practice'. Read it as props.questions ?? props.additionalProps?.questions, top level first. When it is non empty it REPLACES the authored practice bank.
hostProps.initialMode: The mode the tool must open in, fully set up, first beat ready.
hostProps.enabledModes: Which of the four modes exist this session.
hostProps.learnQuestions: TOP LEVEL. The Learn bank for this concept, from question_bank_v2 where delivery_mode = 'Learn', mandatory checkpoints first. Read it as props.learnQuestions ?? props.additionalProps?.learnQuestions. When it is non empty those items ARE the Learn steps; the authored scene examples are only the fallback for a thin pool.
hostProps.showModeSelector: false in production for every maths tool. Honour it, defaulting to true (const showSelector = props.showModeSelector ?? true) so the selector still works in preview and review, and disappears live.
hostProps.additionalProps.exampleSeed: A 32 bit int the tool's mulberry32 PRNG consumes directly. The teacher agent builds its own copy of the example set from the SAME seed, so Math.random(), Date.now() or ignoring the seed desynchronises the narration from the screen in every single session.

questions.description: Replaces the built in practice bank. Items are {kind:'build', target:string} | {kind:'read_board', cells:(number|null)[]} | {kind:'which_zeros', target:string} | {kind:'choice', prompt, options[], correct, explain}.

columnCount.description: How many place columns the board shows, clamped 1 to 7.

showNumberLine.description: Plot the intended and the collapsed number on a line so the size difference is visible rather than stated.

zeroTileSupply.description: Whether zero tiles are available. Starts false so the failure case can happen before the repair.

constraints: The board is modelled as an array of digit or null values and the rendered number is derived from it, so an empty column always collapses and never silently pads.
The tool never inserts a zero the student did not place, in any mode, because the collapse is the lesson.
The readout reads the board aloud in text, so the student hears what they actually wrote rather than what they meant.
Both the intended and the collapsed value are plotted on the same number line whenever they differ, so the error has a size and not just a name.
The stated rule is tested on 5000 and on 5, so a rule that says zeros are always needed and a rule that says they are only needed in the middle both fail.

extra.concept_only: Concept carries no questions of its own. Its beats reveal the idea and then run one reasoning beat each, and every number the agent says is read from state.truth.

ai.shows: The place value board, the readout, the number line, the teacher caption, and discrete step navigation (Prev / Step k of 3 / Next) with a progress bar.
steps: Predict: 3 sits in hundreds, 5 in ones, tens empty, and the readout is HIDDEN. The class commits what number will be read, out loud, and the teacher commits it on the pad. prediction_made unlocks the beat.
Collapse: the readout shows 35 and both 35 and 305 are plotted on the line, so the gap is a distance and not a digit.
Repair: the zero tile drops into tens and the columns re anchor, the 3 returning to 300 and the readout to 305.
ai.done_when: Beat 3 has been reached and the repaired board reads 305. Concept has no Finish button.
ai.driven_by: The teaching agent, through next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) and the component calls.
ai.opens_with: A four column board with 3 in hundreds, 5 in ones, tens empty, no readout and no zero tiles available, the predict pad open on 'You write 3 in hundreds and 5 in ones and leave tens empty. What number will be read?'.

learn.shows: One worked item: the board, the readout, the question, then the collapse or the repair and the answer together.
steps: One beat per bank item, in the order the bank supplies: every mandatory checkpoint first in Easy, Medium, Hard order, then the random Learn slots.
learn.fallback: If props.learnQuestions arrives empty, fall back to the authored set: 305 with the tens left empty, 305 repaired, 3005 with two internal zeros, 5000, and 5.
learn.done_when: The last Learn item has been revealed. No Finish button renders in Learn.
learn.driven_by: The teaching agent, through next() / prev(); the on screen Prev / Next also work for a reviewer.
learn.opens_with: The first mandatory checkpoint from props.learnQuestions, its board already built from the question's own digits.

normal.shows: The board, the readout, the number line, every control, no score and no question.
steps: No steps. Nothing is mandatory and nothing is scored.
normal.done_when: The student presses Finish, which emits finished once.
normal.opens_with: An empty four column board with the full tile supply and every control live.
play_modes: TENFOLD DROP: build a board, take one column out, and check that the reading lost exactly one place.
TWO GAPS: leave two columns empty and find every wrong number one repair can still give.
TRAILING TEST: build a number ending in zeros and remove them one at a time, naming what each removal costs.
RULE HUNT: write your own rule for when a zero is needed, then run it on 5000 and on 5.
normal.parameter_freedom: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.
